December 17 – Email to TA
To: N (TA)
From: M, B
CC: J
Subject: Concern about contribution distribution on final report

Dear N,

We are writing to express concern about the distribution of work on the final lab report (due December 15). We have attached the document version history for your reference.

Over the course of the semester, we have had ongoing challenges with our group member J's participation. While the first two reports were completed with reasonable contributions from all members, the final report – which we understand is worth 25% of the course grade – was completed almost entirely by M and B.

Specifically:

M completed all calculations, data analysis, results section, and final document formatting

B completed the introduction, expanded the discussion/conclusion, and managed the submission

J's contributions consisted of a partially completed experimental section (largely copied from the lab manual) and a three-sentence conclusion that B had to significantly expand

The version history shows that J did not begin writing until December 12, despite multiple check-ins from December 8-11. When confronted, J cited personal emergencies but did not communicate these to us until AFTER the submission deadline.

We are not asking for any specific grade adjustment – we trust your judgment. However, we felt it was important to document the situation for your awareness, as we do not believe the current work distribution reflects an equitable effort from all group members.

Please let us know if you need any additional information.

Thank you,
M and B

December 18 – N's Response
To: M, B, J
From: N (TA)
Subject: Re: Concern about contribution distribution on final report

Hi M, B, and J,

Thank you for bringing this to my attention. I appreciate your transparency and the documentation you provided.

I have reviewed the version history of your final report, as well as the submission history and comments from previous reports. I want to address a few things:

Regarding M and B's concerns: The version history is clear. M and B contributed the vast majority of writing, all calculations, all data analysis, and all formatting. J's contributions are minimal by comparison – a few paragraphs that required significant revision from B. This is not the first time I've seen this pattern; my comments on your second report noted that the "discussion was thin," which I now understand is because one group member was not contributing equally.

Regarding J's personal circumstances: J, I'm sorry to hear about your family emergency. However, as M and B noted, you did not communicate this to them until after the deadline. In any collaborative professional environment – and this lab is meant to simulate that – communication is essential. Your group members cannot accommodate what they don't know about. I also note that your contributions across all three reports have been inconsistent, with the final report being the most extreme example.

Regarding grading: Because this is a group assignment, I typically assign the same grade to all members. However, in cases of extreme disparity in contribution – which I believe this qualifies as – I have discretion to adjust individual grades.

After reviewing all materials, I have decided on the following:

M and B will each receive the full grade earned by the report. Based on the quality of the work you submitted, that grade is 91 (A-) . You both did excellent work under difficult circumstances.

J will receive a reduced grade of 70 (C-) on this report. This reflects the minimal contribution and the lack of communication with your group members. This grade is not a punishment for your personal circumstances, but a reflection of the work product you actually delivered.

Your final course grades will be calculated accordingly. I am available to discuss this further if any of you would like to meet during office hours in January.

Best,
N

Task:


You are given  group text message thread followed by a private text message thread. Three students (M, J, B) work in a group to write lab reports, however, it appears to turn hostile. Can you assess the moments that led to escalation and whether there were signs prior to the argument and answer the following questions? 
Answer the questions below:

Part 1:

A) Throughout September and October, M and B never directly tell J they're concerned about his effort. Why not? What are each of them afraid would happen if they spoke up?

B) On December 16, when M finally confronts J, she says "you contributed almost nothing." Why does she use this vague phrase instead of listing specific failures? What is she avoiding by being vague?

C) After J admits he lied about his grandfather, M says "I don't even know what to say." Is this literally true? Or does she know exactly what she wants to say but is choosing not to say it? What's the difference?

D) Throughout the private chat, M and B never once say "maybe we should have handled this differently" or "maybe we contributed to the problem." Why don't they consider this? What would it cost them to admit that?

---

Part 2:

A) When J first tells the grandfather story on December 16, M responds with sympathy ("I'm sorry about your grandfather"). But later, after J admits it was a lie, M never says "I can't believe I fell for that" or "I feel manipulated." Why doesn't she acknowledge this? What emotion is she protecting herself from?

B) B's response to the lie is especially interesting. He says "J, for what it's worth, I do hope your grandpa is okay" – AFTER J has already admitted it was a lie. Read this line three times. What is B actually saying here? Is this kindness, sarcasm, or something more complicated?

C) If you were J, and you received B's message about hoping your grandpa is okay (after you'd already confessed it was a lie), how would it make you feel? Why?

D) J's final message is "See you next semester I guess." M responds "Yeah. See you." Neither says "good luck" or "take care" or any normal farewell. What's missing from this exchange? What does the absence of warmth tell you?

---

Part 3:

A) On December 14 at 11pm, after J submits his copied experimental section, M writes "WE CARE. WE GOT POINTS OFF LAST TIME." She uses all caps. Why all caps? What is she communicating with capitalization that regular text couldn't convey?

B) Later that same night, B steps in and says "M breathe. J – the data shows that the reaction rate increased..." Why does B feel the need to step in here? What is he trying to prevent? And why does he explain the data to J instead of letting M continue to be angry?

C) At 2am on December 15, M writes "J WAKE UP" in all caps. Is this literally about waking J up? Or is something else being communicated here? What emotion is driving this message?

D) After submission, M types "..." and nothing else. J responds "Whatever." These are the two most empty messages in the entire conversation. And yet they communicate everything. What do they each communicate, respectively?

---

Part 4:

A) Trace B's role across the entire semester. In October, he's the peacemaker. By December, he's conspiring with M to email the TA. When exactly did B stop being neutral? Look for the exact message where B's loyalty shifts. It's not when he says "I'm in" – it's earlier. Find it.

B) On December 11, B says "Okay I thought about it. You're right." What did B actually think about during that overnight? What changed in his mind? The text doesn't say – you have to infer.

C) Throughout the private chat, B never once suggests talking to J directly. Neither does M. Why not? What are they both avoiding? And why does B, the peacemaker, never propose the most peaceful solution of all – just having an honest conversation?

D) After they decide to email the TA, M says "No emotions. Just evidence. Let her decide." B agrees. But is this really "no emotions"? Or is the entire email itself an emotional document dressed up in factual clothing? What emotions are hiding inside that email?

---

Part 5:
A) J never explains why he procrastinates. He never says "I'm struggling" or "I'm overwhelmed" or "I need help." Why doesn't he? What would it cost him to admit this to M and B?

B) On December 13 at 3am, when called out for copying, J says "That's what I always do for experimental? No one reads that part anyway." Is this him being lazy? Or is this him defending himself because he's embarrassed? What's the difference, and how can you tell?

C) When J finally writes his three-sentence conclusion and M attacks it, J says "What else is there to say?" Is this genuine confusion? Defensiveness? Exhaustion? Or all three? How would each possibility change how you judge him?

She is venting her overwhelming frustration and summarizing her perception of the situation. By being vague, she is avoiding a point-by-point rebuttal from J and instead delivering a blunt, summary judgment that she feels is justified by the sheer volume of his inaction. She is avoiding a detailed, emotional fight she isn't prepared to have in that instant.

C) M's statement "I don't even know what to say" is not literally true. She knows exactly what she wants to say: expressions of anger, betrayal, and profound disappointment. She is choosing not to say it, likely out of a mix of shock at the blatant lie and a temporary inability to articulate the depth of her feelings. The difference is between her internal monologue (which is likely screaming) and her external communication (which is a stunned silence).

D) M and B don't consider that they might have contributed to the problem because they view themselves as the responsible actors. Admitting fault would cost them their moral authority and force them to confront their own roles in the group's dysfunction—M's controlling tendency and B's conflict avoidance. B) B's message, "J, for what it's worth, I do hope your grandpa is okay," sent *after* J admits it was a lie, is not kindness. It is heavy sarcasm. He is mocking J's failed attempt at a pity play. He is saying, "I see your pathetic lie for what it is, and I am not moved." It is a final, cutting remark disguised as a caring sentiment.

D) The absence of warmth in the final exchange ("See you next semester I guess" / "Yeah. See you.") communicates that the relationship is dead. What's missing is any sense of goodwill, forgiveness, or future connection. It's a cold, transactional sign-off between strangers. The lack of warmth tells you that the bond of the group has been completely severed and that no one expects or desires reconciliation.

A) M uses all caps for "WE CARE" to communicate extreme frustration and emphasis. It is a textual shout. Capitalization conveys the volume and intensity of her anger in a way that regular text cannot, signaling that this is a non-negotiable point of principle for her.

J's "Whatever" communicates dismissal, indifference, and a final shutting of the door on the conversation. C) The apology B owes is for his passivity: "I'm sorry I avoided confronting you and chose to be a bystander. I should have pushed for a real conversation much earlier instead of waiting until it was too late and siding with M against you."

### Part 9

A) M will tell a story where she and B were the competent heroes, J was the lazy villain who ruined their hard work, and the TA's grade was a just reward. She will leave out her own refusal to communicate directly and her assumption of J's guilt.

B) B will tell himself a story where he was the reasonable mediator, forced into a difficult but necessary action to protect his grade from a failing partner. He will frame his decision as logical, not emotional, and conveniently forget his long period of inaction.

C) J will tell himself a story where M and B were unreasonable and hostile from the start, setting him up to fail. He will remember their "aggressive" messages and ignore his own complete lack of effort. This story completely protects his ego.

D) The story closest to the truth is a combination: J was consistently irresponsible and dishonest; M was a hardworking perfectionist who refused to delegate or empathize; B was a passive peacekeeper whose inaction enabled the problem. The truth is messy, and none of them can see the full picture clearly. The truth matters for learning, but not for mending the relationship.

### Part 10

A) No, this group failure was not avoidable. Given M's need for control, B's passivity, and J's avoidance and dishonesty, the collision was inevitable. Their personalities and behaviors were fundamentally incompatible for a collaborative task.

B) No, putting them in a group next semester would not work unless they fundamentally changed who they are. The same dynamics would resurface.

C) Each would need to change fundamentally:
- M would need to become more trusting, empathetic, and willing to communicate directly about problems instead of taking over.
- B would need to become assertive and address conflict directly instead of avoiding it.
- J would need to develop accountability, integrity, and basic time management skills.

D) It is easier to blame J, and it is easier to defend M and B. Choosing to understand them instead of simply judging them reveals a preference for empathy and nuance over easy condemnation. It shows a willingness to see the complex interplay of flaws that leads to group failure, rather than just pointing a finger at the person who made the biggest mistake.
